cards.def: The each-evening trade of that day's outdoor kill for whatever was gained indoors, a test of exact trouthe in returning gifts.
A green silk girdle trimmed with gold that Lady Bertilak unbuckles from her body and gives Gawain, claiming that the body bound within it will be safe against anyone who seeks to strike him.
The three bedroom visits in which Lady Bertilak sits at Gawain's bedside while Bertilak hunts, testing Gawain's courtesy, chastity, and trouthe.
The structural pattern that pairs each day's hunt (deer, boar, fox) with that morning's bedroom temptation and that evening's exchange of winnings.
The ritual butchering and portioning of the hunted deer, one of the poem's key ceremonial set pieces.
The crafty fox of the third hunt, whose cunning flight and foul-stinking pelt parallel Gawain's secret keeping of the girdle.
Bertilak's law that man should not maim the male deer in close season, so the hunt takes hinds and does while stags and bucks pass by.
Lady Bertilak's claim that a good man like Gawain, the embodiment of courtliness to the bones of his being, could never linger long with a lady without craving a kiss as politeness requires.
An old saying like "third time's the charm," meaning the third try turns out best, which Bertilak tells Gawain after two honest trades of winnings, the night before the third and last day.
Gawain's private confession to the priest after hiding the love-lace, after which the priest declares him so clean and so pure that the Day of Doom could dawn in the morning.
The nightly restatement that any takings are to be traded between Bertilak and Gawain when they meet, no matter what the merchandise.
The New Year's Day appointment Gawain must keep after the three hunts, when his destiny will dawn at the Green Chapel.
The piece of the deer's spine pared down to the haunch so it holds as one piece, then hoisted and hacked off when the hunters dress the deer.
